The engine power or RPM is reduced by lowering the manifold pressure and increasing the blade angle. This is the same process as that used for climbing after takeoff.
The greater mass of air handled per second in this case is more than offset by the lower slipstream velocity and increase in airspeed.
The angle of attack is kept small by the increase in blade angle.
For climbing after takeoff, the power output or RPM of the engine is reduced by decreasing the engine manifold pressure and increasing the blade angle.
High blade angle increases the mass of air handled per revolution. This decreases engine RPM, reducing fuel consumption and engine wear and keeps thrust at a maximum.
After liftoff and as airplane speed increases a high blade angle or pitch keeps the angle of attack small and efficient with respect to the relative wind.

The high RPM also creates maximum thrust required for takeoff. Although the mass of air handled per revolution is small, the revolutions per minute are many, the slipstream velocity is high and with low airplane speed the thrust is maximum.
The light load created by the low blade angle allows the engine to turn at high RPM and convert the maximum amount of fuel into heat energy in a given time.
